+title: Let a restore set the user presence of the restored sessions
+---
+Asked by ACPAgent (its card ^smgadam). The user presence belongs to the current client. A session recorded as interactive and resumed by `acp-agent run --resume` must be headless, and the reverse.
+
+- [ ] `restoreSession` and `restoreSessionTree` get the parameter `userPresence: UserPresence? = nil`. Additive API only.
+- [ ] A value that is not nil overrides the recorded value for the restored root and for each restored child in the tree. One client owns the whole restored tree.
+- [ ] nil keeps the current rule: the recorded value, else `.interactive`.
+- [ ] Fixed-order tests: recorded interactive restored as headless; recorded headless restored as interactive; nil keeps the recorded value (root and child).
+- [ ] One full run. Push when green. Report the head and CI. #elicitation-phase-2
\ No newline at end of file

+  text: 'Research: the public entry point is `RoutedModel.restoreSession(id:...)` in Recording/SessionRestoration.swift. It calls the internal `restoreSessionTree(root:...)` in Recording/SessionTreeRestoration.swift. No other restore entry point exists in Sources (Router has none). Each node gets its presence at `makeSessionToolWiring(... userPresence: configuration?.restoredUserPresence ?? .interactive)`. Discovery: a restored session never writes its sidecar again (`writeSidecarIfNew` is write-once, and a restore writes no sidecar). Thus a second restore with nil gives the value that the sidecar recorded at creation, not the override. The override reaches the disk only through a later fork of the restored session, because the fork copies the presence of the run plane and writes a new sidecar. The tests check this true behavior.'
